newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania Democrats struggle in anti-communist area.
newsitem.headline: Albania Democrats struggle in anti-communist area.

text.p: President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, already dealt a crushing election defeat by the opposition Socialists, was struggling on Sunday to hold on to seats in one of Albania's strongest anti-Communist bastions.
Residents of Kavaje, 50 km (30 miles) southwest of Tirana, say hardline Communist leader Enver Hoxha had it in for their town and its tough traders during four decades in office.
Two years after the 1990 overthrow of communism, voters put Berisha, a free-market advocate, into parliament and then last year elected Democratic Party leader Tritan Shehu.

This time, with Berisha blamed by many Albanians for the loss of their life savings in failed investment schemes, Shehu was one of three members of the right-wing Democrats trying to claw their way back into the assembly in a run-off.

"People are now trusting in God rather than political parties," said Edmond Korbi, the Democratic Party official in charge of polling station No. 6 in Shehu's district -- located in a dilapidated billiard hall.
"When you dance, you change the tune and the step. All this will be for the better. I'm for economic revenge, cracking down on corruption and drugs, not political revenge."
Turnout at three Kavaje polling stations was well down from last week -- sometimes by up to two thirds -- as the contests were seen as having little effect on the overall outcome.

Last week's first round swept more than 80 Socialists into parliament, compared to 20 Democrats. The 34 runoffs on Sunday will determine merely the size of the majority to be held by the Socialists, reformed heirs of Albania's communist party.
Kavaje's city centre bears a plaque dedicated to the man who was shot dead in one of Albania's first street protests that eventually pushed the communists from power.
So solid were the Democrats's credentials here that Berisha chose the city in May to announce the early election aimed at ending the country-wide violence that has killed 1,500 people.
Shehu's opponent is not a Socialist but a schoolteacher from another right-of-centre party, the United Albanian Right.

"History has made us mistrust the man in charge -- the king before the war, Hoxha and now Berisha," said Ismail Kamberi, seated at one of Kavaje's many pavement bars. "That's why we want to make sure other parties get into parliament."
His friend Xhemal Bello said residents had turned away from Berisha after losing what little they had saved in the schemes.
"Berisha is like the dairy cow which produces and produces and produces, but when it comes time to distribute the milk, he kicks over the bucket," he said.

Insistence by locals that March's violence had bypassed the town was belied by the arrival of a man firing a Kalashnikov rifle into the air from the back of a motorbike. A second man fired back from outside another billiard hall across the road.

At Kavaje's market, Alush Celhaga, who makes his living looking after donkeys tethered in an enclosure, also said he would vote against Shehu. Like countless thousands, he lost a stake equivalent to $600 in one of the four failed schemes.
"We had 50 years of communism and now five years of this. If anything, things are worse now," said Celhaga, pocketing a coin worth 15 U.S. cents for each donkey entrusted to him.
"People used to support the Democrats, but they destroyed everything. I'll vote for anything that will bring us closer to the rest of Europe."

Given Kavaje's visceral mistrust of communism, the other two Democrats may fare better as they face Socialist opponents in their run-offs. They include former interior minister Halit Shamata, who also writes poetry.

"I'll vote for Shamata even if he didn't keep promises on improving water supplies and roads," said Fuat, carrying home a brand-new butter churn to replace one worn out after 20 years. "I just can't trust the Socialists after all this time."
